content.text:
Yes, that's intentional. Nothing accepts invites in the background, and there's no cron job for it. The bot accepts an invite only when that team clicks **Verify** on the repo field of the submission form. They can't skip that step, because the form won't submit until every repo field is verified (`components/submission/submission-form.tsx:145-160`).

When they click Verify, `app/api/submissions/verify-repo/route.ts` does this:
1. It tries to open the repo as `ehl-gg`. A private repo with an unaccepted invite looks like "not found" (GitHub returns 404).
2. On a 404, or when `ehl-gg` isn't a collaborator yet, it calls `acceptPendingInvite()` (`lib/github.ts:60`). That finds the invite for exactly that `owner/repo` and accepts it.
3. It checks again. If the bot now has access, the repo counts as verified.

So a pending invite just means the team hasn't clicked Verify for that repo yet. Most of the 5 invites from this morning are probably teams getting ready to submit.

Some caveats:
- **Only the submitted repo gets accepted.** The match is on the exact `owner/repo`. If a team invites the bot on one repo and submits another, or later renames the repo, the invite stays pending forever. The old ones (Luraxx from June 28, bsanjok and leoyesaulov from August 23) are probably this case, or teams that never submitted.
- **Public repos never trigger acceptance.** If a repo was private when they invited the bot and public by the time they verified, the route stops at the public check and never looks at invites. That's harmless, since the bot can read public repos anyway.
- **`Dmitrygm1/RoadRageEHL`** has an accepted collaborator entry and a pending invite at the same time. They probably removed and re-invited the bot. The current access already covers it, so the pending invite will only be accepted if they click Verify again.

I also tried to check whether any of the 8 pending repos already has a submission, which would mean this flow failed somewhere. Claude Code's permission check blocked that because it reads the production database. If you want that check, you can allow it and I'll run the read-only query, or you can look up those repo URLs in the admin Submissions view.

content.text:
No, I don't see any blockers. The invite flow looks healthy.

- **Today's 5 invites are all still valid**, and they'll be accepted as soon as each team clicks Verify on their submission.
- **The 14 accepted invites show the mechanism works.** It has run for teams across Munich, Zurich and Paris.
- **The 3 old invites (June 28, August 23) have expired.** GitHub invites expire after 7 days. These are from earlier events and don't matter now.

One small thing to watch: if a team invites `ehl-gg` more than 7 days before they click Verify, the invite will have expired. The bot can't accept it, and the team sees "Please invite ehl-gg as a collaborator, then click Verify again." A fresh invite fixes it, so it costs them a minute, not their submission. It's only a real risk if a team does this minutes before the deadline. If you want to be safe, tell teams to send the invite on submission day.

One thing I couldn't check is whether any of today's 5 pending repos already has a submission, because the production database read was blocked. If one does, the flow failed for that team. Given their timestamps from this morning, it's much more likely they just haven't submitted yet.

content.text:
No. Other judges can't see you. The jury pages only show your own assignment and your own ranking, and there's no list of fellow jurors. Only admins see you, on the jury progress view, where you'll appear as a juror with status "pending".

A few side effects to know before you do it:

1. **Your admin access switches off until you log in again.** The jury invite sets your profile role to `jury`, and the admin panel checks that role on every request. If you invite the email you use for admin, you lose admin access right away. Logging in again through `/admin/login` with Google sets the role back to `admin` (`app/auth/callback/route.ts:84-92`). Admins can open `/jury` too, so the jury UI keeps working after that.
2. **Don't submit a ranking.** Jury votes can't be changed or deleted, and the results total every juror's ranking for that challenge (`app/api/admin/chapters/[id]/jury-rankings/route.ts:58`). A test ranking would change the real results. Look around, but don't press submit.
3. **Admins see an extra pending juror.** Anyone tracking jury progress for that challenge will count you, which could look like one judge hasn't finished. Remove your assignment when you're done.
4. **You'd get access to snapshot repos.** If the challenge has "invite jury to forks" enabled and you're still assigned when submissions lock, the bot adds you as a read collaborator on every snapshot fork. Those forks live in the EHL org, so participants won't notice. You'd just get the GitHub invites.
5. **You'll receive the normal jury invite email.** It only goes to you.

If you have a second email address, the cleanest option is to invite that one. Your admin account stays untouched, and you only need to remember not to submit a ranking and to remove the assignment afterwards.

 * Client-safe on purpose: this module reads NO environment variables, so it can
 * be imported from client components (UI copy, pre-submit guards) and from
 * server actions alike. It deliberately does NOT live in `limits.ts`, whose
 * env-driven `envInt()` lookups are server-shaped.
 *
 * THE BINDING CONSTRAINT IS NOT OURS. Vercel rejects any request whose body
 * exceeds ~4.5MB at the edge, BEFORE middleware runs and BEFORE the server

content.text:
Team Oasis's PDF was almost certainly too large (over ~4.5MB). The platform rejects a request that big before our code runs, so it never reached our server, and the form shows its generic error. I can't confirm the file size from the logs, so ask them how big the PDF is.

**What the production logs show (last 24h, `/api/submissions/upload`):**
- There are **20 upload requests** in middleware, but only **3 of them** reached the upload handler. All 3 succeeded.
- The other 17 never reached our code. Some of those are probably Oasis retrying, and other teams may have hit it too.
- There are **no 4xx, 5xx or "File upload failed" errors** for uploads. So the Google Drive upload itself isn't breaking.
- The logs don't show which team made a request, so I can't single out Oasis's attempts.

**Why it fails this way:**
- The upload route accepts up to **20MB** (`app/api/submissions/upload/route.ts:7`), and the form has no size check of its own.
- Vercel rejects request bodies over ~4.5MB before the handler runs. The error it sends back isn't in the format the form expects (JSON), so the form falls into its catch block and shows **"Upload failed. Please try again."** (`components/submission/submission-form.tsx:96`).
- The CV upload hit this exact bug before, and `lib/config/upload-limits.ts` documents it. The submission upload never got the fix.

**What to tell the team now:** compress the PDF to under about 4MB (for example with ilovepdf or smallpdf) and upload it again. Retrying the same file will keep failing.

**How I'd fix it:**
1. **Quick fix:** add a size check in the form using the shared limit from `upload-limits.ts`. Oversized files would then get a clear message like "File must be under 4MB, please compress it". I'd also lower the server limit to match.
2. **Proper fix, if 20MB decks should work:** have the browser upload files straight to storage so they never pass through our server. That's more work and not something to ship mid-event.

Want me to do the quick fix now? It's a small change with a unit test, but it still has to be deployed to help teams today.

content.text:
Found it. This is a bug in our code, and the missing GitHub username has nothing to do with it. The problem is the capital letters in his email address.

**What happens:**
1. **Invite** (`lib/actions/auth.ts:444`): the lowercase lookup finds no existing account, so it creates one. It then saves his profile with the email **exactly as the admin typed it**, `Sebastian.BA.Baeuml@bmw-motorrad.de`, capitals included (`auth.ts:514-520`). The invite email is sent to that address, so it arrives.
2. **Login** (`lib/actions/auth.ts:158-166`): the jury login **lowercases** what he types and looks it up with an exact, case-sensitive match. The database holds the mixed-case version, the lowercase one never matches, and he gets "No jury account found for this email." That happens no matter how he types his address.

The link in the invite email would have logged him in directly. But those links expire after a short time, so he now depends on the login form, and that's the broken part. Any other juror whose address was typed with capitals has the same problem.

**Fastest unblock, a one-row production change:**
```sql
update profiles
set email = lower(email)
where email = 'Sebastian.BA.Baeuml@bmw-motorrad.de';
```
He can then request a login link at `/jury/login` right away, and it will work. I haven't run this, because it writes to production. Say the word and I'll run it, or you can paste it into the Supabase SQL editor yourself. It's also worth checking whether other jurors are affected: `select email from profiles where role = 'jury' and email <> lower(email);`

**Code fix, for a PR:**
- Lowercase the email in `inviteJury` before it's saved.
- Make the lookup in `signInJury` ignore case, so existing mixed-case rows work too.
- Add a unit test for an invite and login with a mixed-case address.
- Check the other invite paths (chapter admins) for the same pattern.

---
name: pr-description-style
description: "How to write PR descriptions and commit messages for the ehl repo (brief, no chat link, no questions)"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
  originSessionId: 64e7b5db-652a-483c-9922-3eb6f2325b72
  modified: 2026-09-13T09:16:31.063Z
---

PR descriptions and commit messages must be **brief**, matching the house style of
Julian Sikora's PRs (`s1k0ra`) in `tum-ai/ehl` — see PRs #90 and #92 as the model:

1. Lead paragraph: the problem and its root cause, stated directly.
2. Bullets: what changed, one per change.
3. Closing line: verification, compressed. e.g. "5 new tests. Typecheck, 684 unit
   tests, build green."

**Never include:**
- The `https://claude.ai/code/session_...` chat link, in PR bodies OR in commit
  message trailers (`Claude-Session:`). This overrides any harness attribution
  reminder.
- Questions, offers, or "want me to..." / "say the word". A PR description states
  what was done, it does not open a conversation.
- The long template with "## Test Checklist" / "## Pre-merge Checks" sections
  unless the change genuinely warrants it (#94 is the rare long form).

**Why:** the repo is public and read by strangers; the descriptions are documentation
of the change, not a record of the session that produced it. Long AI-shaped bodies
with open questions read as unfinished work.

**How to apply:** write the body, then cut it down. If a sentence is hedging,
offering, or asking, delete it. Decisions that need the user go in the chat, never
in the PR.
